Saffron
SAF-ron
n. (a costly yellow spice from the crocus flower)
Hebrew karkom, saffron, from a root meaning to be yellow; the Arabic zafaran gives the English by way of Old French. The spice is the dried stigma of the crocus, three threads to a flower, which is why it has always been among the costliest substances by weight.

Biblical Definition

Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices. The single mention of saffron in Scripture stands in a catalogue, and the catalogue is a description of the bride — an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits; camphire, with spikenard. Every item named is expensive and every one is imported. Spikenard came from the Himalayas, cinnamon and calamus from the east, frankincense and myrrh from Arabia; saffron requires a field of crocuses for an ounce. The Song is not compiling a herbal. It is saying, by an accumulation of costly things, what the beloved is worth to the one who speaks. This is how Scripture ordinarily handles spices: they are the vocabulary of value. The same substances appear in the holy anointing oil and the incense of the sanctuary, where their costliness is precisely the point, and they appear again in the gifts brought to the infant Christ. The dictionary reads the Song as what it presents itself to be — the celebration of covenanted love between a husband and wife — and receives the long typological tradition of the church, which has heard in it Christ and his bride, as a true and secondary reading built on that literal foundation rather than a replacement for it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a plant of the genus Crocus, the stigmas of which are used in medicine and as a yellow dye; a deep yellow colour.

expand to see more

SAFFRON, n. A plant of the genus Crocus; the flower has a long tube and a large erect border.

SAFFRON, n. The stigmas of the flower, dried, used as a medicine, a condiment, and a yellow dye.

SAFFRON, a. Having the color of saffron flowers; deep yellow.

SPIKENARD, n. A plant of the genus Nardus; an aromatic and highly esteemed ointment prepared from it.

SPICE, n. A vegetable production, fragrant or aromatic to the smell and pungent to the taste, used in sauces and in cookery.

Key Scripture

Song of Solomon 4:14 — "Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices:"

Song of Solomon 4:13 — "Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits; camphire, with spikenard,"

Song of Solomon 1:17 — "The beams of our house are cedar, and our rafters of fir."

Isaiah 61:10 — "I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels."

Modern Corruption

The Song is handled either by allegorising away its plain subject or by reducing it to ancient love poetry with no place in revelation; the dictionary holds the literal sense and the church's typology together.

expand to see more

The older error, running from Origen through much of the medieval church, was embarrassment at the literal text: the Song was allegorised so thoroughly that its subject — the love of a husband and wife — disappeared, and every spice became a code for a doctrine. The Reformers pruned this back hard, and rightly. Scripture's own doctrine of marriage does not need rescuing from Scripture's own celebration of it. Solomon's catalogue of costly spices says that the bride is precious, and a reading that cannot say so plainly has lost the foundation on which every further sense must be built.

The modern error is the opposite and more corrosive: the Song treated as recovered Near Eastern love poetry, canonical by accident, with no prophetic or typological weight at all. That surrenders what the whole of Scripture builds on the marriage figure — the LORD as husband to Israel, Christ as bridegroom to his church, the marriage supper of the Lamb at the end. Isaiah reaches for a bridegroom and bride to describe salvation itself. The Song's literal subject is honourable and real, and it is also the pattern God chose for his covenant love, which is why Solomon's saffron and spikenard have always sounded to the church like more than a shopping list.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew karkom (H3750), saffron; nerd (H5373), spikenard; qinnamown (H7076), cinnamon; besem (H1314), spice or sweet odour.

expand to see more

Hebrew karkom (H3750) — saffron; its only occurrence in Scripture.

Hebrew nerd (H5373) — spikenard; the ointment poured on the Lord's head at Bethany.

Hebrew qaneh (H7070) — calamus, sweet cane; an ingredient of the holy anointing oil.

Hebrew qinnamown (H7076) — cinnamon; likewise in the anointing oil of Exodus 30.

Hebrew besem (H1314) — spice, balsam, sweet savour; rendered chief spices.

Usage

"“Spikenard and saffron” — the costliest goods, named as a measure of worth."

"“with all the chief spices” — the catalogue closed with a superlative."

"“an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits” — the figure the spices belong to."
